formation.title: The Dawn of Kurdistan
formation.text:
The Kurdish people have long dwelt among the mountain fastnesses of the Zagros and Taurus, their tribal confederacies governing valleys that empires could never fully subdue. From the legacy of Saladin's Ayyubid dynasty to the autonomous emirates that carved their own domains between Ottoman and Safavid power, the Kurds have maintained an identity forged in highland stone and tempered by centuries of warfare.

Now, with the formation of Kurdistan, a new chapter begins. The question facing the nation is fundamental: shall Kurdistan draw upon its martial heritage and project power outward as Saladin once did, or shall it consolidate the fractious emirates into a unified state whose strength lies in governance and cultural identity?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We shall carry the sword of Saladin!

modifiers.name: Legacy of Saladin
modifiers.text: The blood of the Ayyubids flows through Kurdish veins. From the mountains of Kurdistan, the warriors who once united the Islamic world under Saladin now ride again, carrying his martial legacy into a new age of conquest.

options.text: We shall unite the emirates as one people.

modifiers.name: Unity of the Emirates
modifiers.text: The Kurdish emirates (Soran, Baban, Bitlis, Bohtan, Ardalan) have long governed their mountain valleys with proud independence. Now united under a single banner, their collective wisdom in governance and diplomacy forges a state greater than any single principality.

advances.name: Mountain Strongholds
advances.text: The Kurdish highlands are dotted with ancient fortresses, Amadiya perched on its precipitous rock outcrop, Hasankeyf overlooking the Tigris from sheer limestone cliffs, positions that have defied invaders for millennia.

advances.name: Tribal Confederacy
advances.text: Kurdish governance has long operated through confederacies of tribes, each headed by an agha or beg, united under paramount chiefs who balance autonomy with collective defense.

advances.name: Kurdish Horsemanship
advances.text: The Kurdish plateau bred both skilled horsemen and hardy mountain horses. Kurdish cavalry served under the Ayyubids, fighting from Damascus to Egypt.

advances.name: Ayyubid Legacy
advances.text: Saladin al-Ayyubi, born of the Kurdish Rawadiya clan, founded a dynasty that united Egypt and Syria and recaptured Jerusalem. His legacy of martial prowess and just governance defines Kurdish identity.

advances.name: Highland Shepherds
advances.text: The seasonal migration of Kurdish herders between highland summer pastures and lowland winter grazing grounds sustained an economy of wool, cheese, and livestock that predated the empires.

advances.name: Frontier Raiders
advances.text: Kurdish tribesmen on the frontiers between great empires developed raiding into an art form, striking from mountain passes and disappearing into terrain no pursuer could navigate.

advances.name: Caravan Waystations
advances.text: The mountain passes of Kurdistan straddle the overland trade routes between Mesopotamia, Persia, and Anatolia. Kurdish waystations provided shelter, fodder, and protection for merchants crossing the highlands.

advances.name: Sheikhs of the Qadiriya
advances.text: The Qadiri order takes root in the Kurdish highlands through families of sayyids such as the Barzinji, who keep a tekiye in each valley. The sheikh feeds the traveller, shelters the fugitive, and is asked to judge between tribes at feud.

advances.name: Mountain Ambush Tactics
advances.text: Kurdish warriors perfected the art of mountain ambush, striking from above in narrow defiles where superior numbers count for nothing and knowledge of the terrain is worth more than any fortification.

advances.name: Emirate Courts
advances.text: The courts of the Kurdish emirs (Bitlis, Soran, Ardalan, Baban) were centers of Persian and Kurdish poetry, historical scholarship, and artistic patronage that rivaled many a royal court.

advances.name: Kurdish Bowmen
advances.text: Kurdish archers, trained from youth in the mountain valleys, could loose arrows from positions no cavalry could reach and no infantry could storm.

advances.name: Chaldiran Alliance
advances.text: The alliance between twenty Kurdish emirs and Sultan Selim I at the Battle of Chaldiran secured Kurdish autonomy within the Ottoman framework and proved Kurdish cavalry decisive in a clash of empires.

event.title: The Alliance at Chaldiran
event.text:
In the summer of 1514, the Kurdish scholar and statesman Idris Bitlisi accomplished what no diplomat before him had managed: the unification of over twenty Kurdish emirs under a single military banner. Leveraging the Kurds' Sunni faith against the encroaching Safavid Shia state, Bitlisi persuaded the highland lords that their future lay with the Ottoman Sultan Selim I.

Kurdish cavalry proved decisive at the Battle of Chaldiran, where their knowledge of the terrain and fierce fighting turned the Ottoman flank against Shah Ismail's forces. In recognition, Selim sent fifteen banners and five hundred royal robes to the Kurdish princes, formalizing an arrangement of autonomy that would endure for centuries.

This alliance secured Kurdish self-governance within the Ottoman framework, the emirs retained hereditary rule, their own courts, and control of the mountain passes. It was not submission but partnership, bought with Kurdish blood on the battlefield.

options.text: The pact is sealed in blood and honor.

modifiers.name: Pact of Chaldiran
modifiers.text: The alliance forged between Kurdish emirs and the Ottoman Sultan at the Battle of Chaldiran secured Kurdish autonomy and military prestige. Kurdish cavalry proved decisive, and the pact endures as proof that Kurdish arms command respect.

options.text: We need no allies; our mountains are our strength.

modifiers.name: Kurdish Self-Reliance
modifiers.text: The mountains of Kurdistan are fortress enough. Without allies to please or obligations to honor, the Kurdish people stand alone, and stand strong.

advances.name: Diyarbakir Citadel
advances.text: The basalt walls of Diyarbakir stretch over five kilometers, standing thirty feet high and sixteen feet thick, among the most formidable fortifications in the Middle East, a UNESCO World Heritage site of enduring military significance.

advances.name: The Sharafnama
advances.text: The Sharafnama of 1597, written by Prince Sharaf Khan Bidlisi, is the first comprehensive history of the Kurdish nation, a chronicle of dynasties, battles, and traditions that gave literary form to Kurdish identity.

event.title: The Sharafnama
event.text:
In 1597, Prince Sharaf Khan Bidlisi of the Bitlis Emirate completed his monumental work, the Sharafnama, the first comprehensive history of the Kurdish nation. Written in Persian to reach the widest possible audience, the Sharafnama chronicles the great Kurdish dynasties from antiquity through the Ayyubid golden age to the autonomous emirates of his own time.

The work documents the Marwanids of Amed, the Hasanwayhids, the Fadluyids, and above all the house of Saladin, weaving them into a single narrative of Kurdish civilization. For the first time, the story of the Kurdish people exists not in fragments of memory and oral tradition, but as a written record that can endure across generations.

The Sharafnama is both history and declaration, a statement that the Kurdish nation possesses a past worthy of its mountains, and a future deserving of recognition.

options.text: Our history shall endure in ink as in stone.

advances.name: Silk Road Tolls
advances.text: Kurdish emirates levied tolls on the caravans crossing their mountain passes between Mesopotamia and Persia, turning geography into revenue and making Kurdish goodwill essential for overland commerce.

advances.name: Irregular Warfare
advances.text: Kurdish fighters developed warfare suited to their terrain, mobile, decentralized, striking from positions that regular armies could not reach and retreating into mountains they knew like their own homes.

advances.name: Baban Governance
advances.text: The Baban emirate, centered on Sulaimani from 1784, developed sophisticated administrative systems that combined tribal tradition with Ottoman bureaucratic practice, governing the Kurdish heartland for two centuries.

advances.name: Kurdish Mounted Regiments
advances.text: Kurdish cavalry served in Ottoman campaigns across the Middle East, bringing mountain horsemanship and fierce tribal loyalty to imperial wars from Baghdad to the Caucasus.

advances.name: Medreses of the Emirs
advances.text: The Kurdish emirs endow medreses beside their courts, as the lords of Botan did with the Red Medrese of Cizre and the lords of Bahdinan with the Qubahan of Amadiya. Their students read law in Arabic and verse in Kurdish, and from them come the jurists and poets of the emirates.

advances.name: Border Autonomy
advances.text: Kurdish emirs maintained self-governance at the Ottoman-Safavid frontier, their autonomy guaranteed by their military value as guardians of the mountain passes between empires.

advances.name: Peshmerga Tradition
advances.text: Peshmerga, 'those who face death', describes the Kurdish warrior ethos. From tribal border guards to organized fighters, the peshmerga tradition represents disciplined, selfless dedication to the defense of Kurdish lands.

advances.name: Tribal Modernization
advances.text: The transformation of Kurdish tribal governance toward more centralized administrative structures, adopting modern methods of taxation, education, and military organization while preserving tribal identity.

advances.name: Mountain Fortifications
advances.text: Systematic fortification of Kurdish mountain passes and strategic heights, building on millennia of defensive architecture from Urartu through the medieval emirate period to create comprehensive highland defense networks.

advances.name: Highland Trade Networks
advances.text: Kurdish merchants connected the towns and cities of the highlands through trade networks that moved wool, livestock, metalwork, and agricultural goods across the mountain terrain.

advances.name: Kurdish Printing
advances.text: The spread of printing technology enabled the dissemination of Kurdish literature and historical works, strengthening cultural identity and literacy across the scattered mountain communities.

advances.name: National Awakening
advances.text: The emergence of a self-conscious Kurdish national identity, drawing on the literary heritage of the Sharafnama, the martial traditions of the peshmerga, and the shared experience of mountain autonomy.

advances.name: Modern Irregulars
advances.text: Kurdish irregular fighters adapted to modern warfare while retaining their mountain advantages, combining knowledge of terrain with modern arms to create forces that conventional armies could not suppress.

advances.name: Highland Industry
advances.text: The development of industrial capacity in Kurdish highland cities, processing local raw materials and producing goods for both domestic consumption and regional trade.

advances.name: Constitutional Movement
advances.text: Kurdish participation in constitutional and reform movements, seeking formal recognition of Kurdish rights and governance within evolving political frameworks.

destiny.name: Destiny of Kurdistan
destiny.text: Kurdistan has risen from the mountain passes. The question now is whether this nation will follow the martial path of Saladin or build strength through the unity of its emirate traditions.

event.title: The Destiny of Kurdistan
event.text: Kurdistan has taken its first steps on the road to greatness. The mountain passes that sheltered our forebears now mark the boundaries of a nation with ambitions that reach beyond any valley. Whether through conquest or governance, the Kurdish people stand ready to carve their destiny into the stones of history.

options.text: Our destiny begins in these mountains.

destiny.name: The Gates of Nineveh
destiny.text: Mosul and Erbil, the great cities of upper Mesopotamia, must fall under Kurdish dominion. These ancient seats of power command the Tigris valley and open the road to Syria.

conditions.text: Own Mosul, or a subject owns it
Own Erbil, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Gates of Nineveh
event.text:
The ancient cities of upper Mesopotamia, Mosul, with its bridges spanning the Tigris, and Erbil, whose citadel has been continuously inhabited for over six thousand years, now answer to Kurdish authority. From these commanding positions, the road to Syria lies open before us.

The last time Kurdish arms held such power in Mesopotamia, Saladin himself rode at their head. That legacy now lives again.

options.text: Mosul and Erbil are ours. Syria awaits.

destiny.name: The Syrian March
destiny.text: Aleppo, jewel of northern Syria, and Mardin, fortress of the Artukids, must answer to Kurdish authority. Saladin's heirs press southward along the routes their ancestors rode.

conditions.text: Own Aleppo, or a subject owns it
Own Mardin, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Syrian March
event.text:
Aleppo's great citadel and Mardin's clifftop fortress have submitted to Kurdish sovereignty. The Ayyubid heirs have reclaimed the northern reaches of their ancestral domain, the trade routes between Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean now run through Kurdish lands.

Our armies stand at the threshold of the Levant. The question is how we press forward: with the fury of holy war, or with the measured hand of frontier lords building lasting dominion.

options.text: With fire and faith, we march south.

modifiers.name: Northern Jihad
modifiers.text: Kurdish armies sweep through Syria with the zeal of holy warriors, storming fortifications and pressing the offensive with little regard for cost. The military momentum is unstoppable, but sustained campaigning weighs on the people.

modifiers.name: Frontier Lords
modifiers.text: Rather than rushing south, Kurdish frontier lords methodically extend their authority through negotiated submissions and rapid garrisoning. Subject populations are pacified quickly, though the focus on military administration diverts resources from civilian needs.

destiny.name: The Ayyubid Restoration
destiny.text: Damascus, Jerusalem, and Cairo, the three pillars of Saladin's empire. To hold them all is to restore the Ayyubid domain in full, a Kurdish dynasty ruling from the Nile to the Zagros.

conditions.text: Own Damascus, or a subject owns it
Own Jerusalem, or a subject owns it
Own Cairo, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Ayyubid Restoration
event.text:
Damascus, Jerusalem, and Cairo, the three pillars upon which Saladin built his empire, all fly the Kurdish banner once more. The restoration of the Ayyubid domain is complete. From the banks of the Nile to the peaks of the Zagros, Kurdish authority is unchallenged.

This achievement demands a statement of purpose. Shall Kurdistan claim the mantle of leadership over the Islamic world, as Saladin did when he united the faithful against the Crusaders? Or shall we style ourselves guardians of the holy places, protectors rather than conquerors?

options.text: We are the Sultans of Islam reborn.

modifiers.name: Sultan of Islam
modifiers.text: Kurdistan claims the mantle of Islamic leadership, echoing Saladin's role as unifier of the faithful. Religious prestige and political authority reinforce each other, and even heretical communities find a place under Kurdish tolerance.

options.text: We shall be guardians of the holy places.

modifiers.name: Guardian of Jerusalem
modifiers.text: Rather than claiming universal authority, Kurdistan positions itself as guardian of the holy places, rebuilding war-torn lands, maintaining fortress networks, and projecting quiet power through intelligence rather than proclamation.

destiny.name: The Baban Consolidation
destiny.text: The Baban emirate centered on Sulaymaniyah pioneered sophisticated Kurdish governance. Secure the heartland, raise Sulaymaniyah into a town fit to be the seat of government, and prove that Kurdish unity can be forged through law, not just the sword.

conditions.text: Own As Sulaymaniyah, or a subject owns it
Sulaymaniyah is ours and has grown into a town

event.title: The Baban Consolidation
event.text:
The work of the Baban emirs lives on in the governance of Kurdistan. Sulaymaniyah, the city they founded and nurtured, serves as proof that Kurdish administration can build lasting prosperity. Law codes, tax registers, and diplomatic channels now bind the emirates together more firmly than any oath of tribal allegiance.

The foundations are laid. What rises upon them will determine whether Kurdistan endures for an age or for eternity.

options.text: The emirates stand united in law.

destiny.name: The Sharaf Khan Legacy
destiny.text: As Sharaf Khan Bidlisi chronicled Kurdish greatness in the Sharafnama, so too must Kurdistan now prove its civilizational depth, through prosperity, prestige, command of the highland economy, and a madrasa at Bitlis where Kurdish scholars write their nation's history.

conditions.text: We own Bitlis and a Madrasa or an Emir's Medrese stands there (Bitlis must first be a town)
A market the country is in

children.text: Wool is produced in the market
Wool is traded in the market

event.title: The Sharaf Khan Legacy
event.text:
Kurdistan has achieved what Sharaf Khan Bidlisi could only chronicle, a prosperous, prestigious Kurdish state whose cultural achievements match its political ambitions. The highland economy thrives, wool flows through mountain markets, and Kurdish scholars debate in courts that command respect.

This moment calls for a choice of emphasis. Shall we invest in the scholars and madrasas that preserve Kurdish knowledge, or in the mountain merchants whose caravans carry Kurdish goods to distant markets?

options.text: The pen is mightier than the purse.

modifiers.name: Highland Scholars
modifiers.text: Kurdish madrasas and scholarly circles flourish, producing graduates who serve as administrators, jurists, and poets. The highland economy benefits from educated governance, and the population grows as prosperity spreads.

modifiers.name: Mountain Merchants
modifiers.text: Kurdish merchants extend their reach across the highland trade routes, bringing wealth back to mountain communities. The cost of this commercial expansion is felt in higher borrowing costs as credit flows outward.

destiny.name: The Kurdish Homeland
destiny.text: The ultimate achievement of the emirate path: a Kurdistan so prosperous and well-governed that it stands as a permanent homeland, three of the old emirates bound to it as subjects under their own princes, its markets humming with silk and commerce.

conditions.text: A market the country is in

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

event.title: The Kurdish Homeland
event.text:
Kurdistan has become everything the scattered emirates once dreamed of, a permanent homeland, prosperous and well-governed, its institutions rooted deep in mountain soil. The great powers may have their empires, but Kurdistan has something more durable: a nation built on the bedrock of shared identity and competent governance.

The final question is one of political philosophy. Shall Kurdistan embrace the confederal traditions of its emirate past, where autonomous provinces govern themselves within a loose union? Or shall it experiment with constitutional forms that channel popular sovereignty, a mountain republic unlike any the world has seen?

options.text: The confederacy endures, as our mountains do.

modifiers.name: Eternal Confederacy
modifiers.text: Kurdistan embraces its confederal heritage, granting each emirate province autonomy within a loose but durable union. Diplomacy and supply networks bind the confederation together without centralizing authority.

modifiers.name: Mountain Republic
modifiers.text: Kurdistan experiments with constitutional governance, an innovative, liberal polity where free subjects participate in governance. A highland republic unlike any the old empires imagined.

units.name: Kurdish Tribal Cavalry
units.text: Light cavalry drawn from the Kurdish tribal confederacies, skilled in raiding and reconnaissance across mountain and plateau terrain.

units.name: Highland Raiders
units.text: Kurdish mountain fighters who strike from hidden positions in highland passes, using terrain advantage to overcome superior numbers.

units.name: Kurdish Bowmen
units.text: Skilled archers trained in the mountain valleys, capable of delivering accurate fire from positions that cavalry cannot reach and infantry cannot storm.

units.name: Mountain Ambushers
units.text: Guerrilla fighters specializing in mountain ambush tactics, using narrow defiles and rocky terrain to devastating effect against conventional forces.

units.name: Chaldiran Cavalry
units.text: Heavy Kurdish cavalry modeled on the riders who fought alongside the Ottomans at Chaldiran, combining tribal ferocity with organized battlefield discipline.

units.name: Mountain Artillery
units.text: Light artillery adapted for mountain warfare, designed to be transported through narrow passes and deployed on heights overlooking enemy positions.

units.name: Peshmerga
units.text: Disciplined mountain infantry embodying the peshmerga tradition, those who face death. Skilled in defensive fighting and mountain warfare, they are the backbone of Kurdish resistance.

units.name: Modern Kurdish Irregulars
units.text: Fast-moving guerrilla infantry combining modern arms with traditional Kurdish knowledge of mountain terrain, striking from positions conventional forces cannot reach.

buildings.name: Mountain Stronghold
buildings.text: A fortified mountain position in the Kurdish highland tradition, using natural terrain to create a defensive strongpoint that commands the surrounding valleys.

buildings.name: Caravan Waystation
buildings.text: A waystation on the mountain trade routes, providing shelter, fodder, and security for caravans crossing Kurdish territories between Mesopotamia and Persia.

buildings.name: Qadiri Tekiye
buildings.text: The house of a Qadiri sheikh. Tribes at feud bring their quarrel here, and the sheikh's word settles the blood money and the grazing bounds. The poor are fed at its door, and the dervishes hold their dhikr in its hall.

buildings.name: Kurdish Citadel
buildings.text: A major urban fortification in the tradition of Diyarbakir's legendary basalt walls, thick, tall, and built to withstand siege for generations.

buildings.name: Emir's Medrese
buildings.text: A school endowed by a Kurdish emir beside his court. Its mullahs teach law and grammar, and its students copy and recite the Kurdish verse of Malaye Jaziri and Ahmad Khani, so that the language of the mountains has books of its own.

buildings.name: Highland Trade Post
buildings.text: A trading hub in the Kurdish highlands, connecting mountain communities with regional markets and facilitating the exchange of wool, livestock, and metalwork.

buildings.name: Highland Forge
buildings.text: An industrial workshop in the Kurdish highlands, processing local iron and copper into tools, weapons, and trade goods for the regional economy.

buildings.name: Zozan
buildings.text: A summer camp on the high pastures. The herding tribes leave their winter quarters in spring, climb with their flocks to the zozan, and return in autumn with the wool.

children.text: The location's raw material is Wool
The location's raw material is Livestock

buildings.name: Kurdish Printing House
buildings.text: A press set up beside an emir's medrese. The verse of Ahmad Khani and Malaye Jaziri, long copied by hand in the students' cells, is printed here.

buildings.name: Ayyubid Palace
buildings.text: A grand palace in the Ayyubid tradition, combining martial fortification with courtly splendor. Its halls echo with the memory of Saladin's court, where warriors and scholars gathered under Kurdish patronage.

buildings.name: Emirate Chancellery
buildings.text: A center of Kurdish governance and administration, where the traditions of the emirate courts are preserved and modernized. Scholars, diplomats, and merchants work under one roof to manage the affairs of the united Kurdistan.

list.name: Hakim Sancaks
list.text: The hereditary Kurdish governorships established by Selim I after the Battle of Chaldiran (1514), on the diplomatic counsel of Idris-i Bidlisi. Unlike the standard Ottoman sancak (rotated, bureaucratically appointed), the great Kurdish emirates of Hakkari, Bitlis, Cizre/Bohtan, and Imadiya/Bahdinan were registered as ocaklik: hereditary in the local mir's house, exempt from devshirme, retaining their tribal contingents, internal courts, and tax discretion. The settlement gave the Sublime Porte a loyal eastern frontier; it gave the Kurdish mirs a constitutional shield around their autonomy that endured into the nineteenth century.

list.name: Sharafnama Register
list.text: The genealogical-political chronicle Prince Sharaf Khan of Bitlis completed in Persian in 1597, treating the Marwanids of Amed, the Hasanwayhids, the Fadluyids, the Ayyubids of Saladin, and every contemporary Kurdish dynasty as one continuous civilization. Maintained as a state institution, the register fixed the genealogical claims of every great house, settled questions of precedence at the mirate court, and gave the Kurdish nation a documented past coextensive with its mountain geography. Later chroniclers continued and recopied the work; it remained the closest thing the Kurdish polity had to a chancery archive of its own past.

list.name: Naqshbandi-Khalidi Tariqat
list.text: The Sufi order reformed and propagated by Mawlana Khalid al-Shahrazuri (d. 1827) of Sulaymaniyah, which by the mid-nineteenth century supplanted the older Qadiriya as the dominant religious network across Kurdistan. The Khalidi sheikhs governed extensive lodges (tekiyes), trained chains of disciples, and as the great mirate houses dissolved one by one under Ottoman centralization, the agha-sheikh combination took up local arbitration, tribal mediation, and even tax collection. By the late Ottoman era the Naqshbandi sheikhs had become the real power-brokers of Kurdish society, often explicitly at the expense of the surviving mir families they replaced.

list.name: Mirate Diwan
list.text: The deliberative council of a Kurdish emirate, most fully developed at Bitlis under the Sharafnama dynasty, at Sanandaj under the long-ruling Ardalans, and at Sulaymaniyah under the Babans. The mir presided over a council of his clan's senior aghas, the chief qadi of the emirate, and the masters of the tribal contingents; the diwan registered grants, heard appeals, and mustered the cavalry of the realm. Where the Hakim sancak settlement preserved the mir's autonomy from Istanbul, the diwan organized that autonomy from within, blending tribal custom with Islamic adjudication and giving Kurdish aristocratic rule its working administrative shape.
